Abstract
The swift and far-reaching evolution of advanced nanostructures and nanotechnologies has accelerated the research 
rate and extent, which has a huge prospect for the benefit of the practical demands of solid-state hydrogen storage 
implementation. Carbonaceous materials are of paramount importance capable of forming versatile structures and 
morphology. This review aims to highlight the influence of the carbon material structure, dimension, and morphology 
on the hydrogen storage ability. An extensive range of synthesis routes and methods produces diverse micro/nano-
structured materials with superb hydrogen-storing properties. The structures of carbon materials used for hydrogen 
adsorption, from 0 to 3D, and fabrication methods and techniques are discussed. Besides highlighting the striking merits 
of nanostructured materials for hydrogen storage, remaining challenges and new research avenues are also considered.

Keywords  Carbonaceous materials · Hydrogen storage · Morphology · Hybrid structure

1  Introduction

High research interest in the development of sustainable and efficient technology for energy storage is induced by a 
ubiquitous demand for energy and the established environmental crisis by the prevailing use of fossil fuels [1]. Hydrogen 
is of paramount interest as an alternative to conventional fossil fuels owing to its high energy density and carbon-free 
combustion products [2].

The hydrogen storage is one of the unwelcome issues in the development of hydrogen energy. Although hydrogen 
is an energy-intensive and environmentally benign energy carrier that holds great promise to meet long-term storage 
targets, the application of hydrogen will become stagnant unless impediments like its production, storage, and trans-
portation are resolved [3].

Hydrogen storage conditions determine the energy cost of a method: the higher the hydrogen pressure and the differ-
ence between the storage temperature and the ambient temperature, the higher the energy cost. The optimal method 
should combine high hydrogen storage density with low energy consumption [4]. To pave the way to a practically viable 
hydrogen storage system, the low total mass of the storage system is essential [5, 6].

The underlying target of developing hydrogen storage materials is to enable their safe distribution to other sectors 
while also stronging usage as onboard fuel cell cars at ambient temperature. There are technical targets for onboard

Cells and Hydrogen Joint Undertaking (FCH JU) in Europe, and the New Energy and Industrial Technology Development 
Organization (NEDO) (NEDO, 2015) in Japan. Based on these targets, the gravimetric density of hydrogen and cost should 
be around 6.5 wt% and 266 USD/kg (Table 1). Currently, no materials can meet the requirements.

Creating a storage technology that is competitive, compact, and ecologically sustainable will enhance the ability of 
hydrogen to rival natural and synthetic fuels in the market effectively. At present, the most widely utilized and commer-
cially available hydrogen storage technologies are compressed gas and liquid storage. However, there is a rapidly grow-
ing interest in emerging solid-state hydrogen storage materials as alternative solutions. Hydrogen can be implemented 
into porous materials or metal hydrides via chemisorption and physicochemical or physisorption interactions [7]. While 
chemisorption interaction, which mainly occurs in metal hydrides, is based on a vigorous reaction with hydrogen mol-
ecules [7], physisorption (porous materials such as zeolites, MOFs, activated carbon, and other carbon-based materials) 
occurs through weak and long-range interactions. Thus, physical–chemical interaction is considered the most pertinent 
for the development of solid hydrogen storage materials because, according to DOE [7], it requires an appropriate range 
of temperature (− 40 to 85 °C) and pressure (< 100 atm) for on-board purposes.

Carbon materials are highly promising for hydrogen storage due to their high stability, low cost, and scalability. 
However, their reliance on physisorption limits their hydrogen storage capacity at ambient conditions compared to 
chemisorption-based materials like metal and complex hydrides. Among the porous materials extensively studied, MOFs 
and COFs stand out due to their tunable structures, high crystallinity, and consistent synthesis processes [8]. Their excep-
tionally high surface area makes them particularly appealing for hydrogen storage applications. Additionally, MOFs offer 
unique merits through the presence of metal binding sites and the ability to post-synthetically modify linkers, setting 
them apart from other porous materials. However, a significant drawback of MOFs, COFs, and porous polymers like PIMs 
lies in their limitations. Despite their high surface area, these materials often suffer from relatively poor chemical and 
thermal stability, as well as obstacles in achieving sustainable large-scale synthesis [8].

In contrast, porous carbon presents a cost-effective alternative. It can be synthesized more easily on an industrial scale 
and derived from recyclable, carbon-rich waste materials, comprising bio-based precursors. Recently, porous carbons 
have garnered significant attention due to their numerous advantages over other materials. Their superior chemical and 
thermal stability compared to MOFs and porous polymers, along with a wide range of optimization strategies to enhance 
hydrogen storage capacity, make them a promising choice for practical applications.

Due to their unique geometry, super conductivity, and adjustable micro-structure, functional carbon materials have 
been extensively introduced into hydrogen storage systems as host materials, barrier layers, and catalyzers. In addition, 
considerable attention has been given to carbon-based materials owing to their low cost, low weight, high surface area, 
high chemical stability, morphologies variations, and specific interaction between gas molecules and carbon atoms as 
potential hydrogen storage materials [9]. Carbon-based materials can densely pack the hydrogen gas molecules with 
protection and persistence. Figure 1 reveals their advantages and disadvantages.

It is well known that a hydrogen molecule forms a link with a typical carbon-based arrangement by mild van der 
Waals interactions, with an energy range of 0.04 to 0.12 eV [10]. In this case, most carbon atoms are in  sp2 hybridization. 
In contrast, when a hydrogen atom reacts chemically with a carbon atom, orbital hybridization shifts from  sp2 to  sp3, 
producing a binding energy between 2 and 3 eV Fig. 2.

Moreover, a computational study has shown that graphene or carbon nanotubes have the potential to be used as 
hydrogen storage materials [11]. Earlier studies reported that the higher electron affinity of carbon nanoparticles depends 
on the structure of carbon-based materials. As demonstrated in Fig. 3, a higher number of pores, folding, and angles, 
and higher electron affinity make the Desorption of hydrogen easier [12].

Carbon atoms can form covalent bonds with three, five, or seven adjacent carbon atoms, potentially creating pentago-
nal and heptagonal surfaces. These surface configurations facilitate the presence of intricate solids and large molecules

2   Techniques for developing carbon materials

2.1   Physisorption of hydrogen

Adsorption occurs when molecules of gases and vapors are attracted to solid surfaces. Physical adsorption of gas mol-
ecules on the surface of a solid results from resonance fluctuations in the charge distribution. Physisorption involves a gas 
molecule interacting with multiple atoms on a solid surface. Physisorption can also be called dispersion compounding 
with short-range repulsive contact between phases, referred to as van der Waals interaction. Another argument made 
by Panella et al. [32] is that forces with the long-range act on the molecules, changing their charge distribution. This, in 
turn, causes increased induced dipoles and starts the interaction. Still, as the electron clouds from close neighbors are 
interpenetrated, nearby gas particles are more repelled by one another.

In the gas–solid system, the Lennard–Jones potential may be applied to show the interaction between the adsorbent 
and the gas molecules. Figure 6 shows the energy vs. distance scale from the adsorbent surface regarding the poten-
tial energy of chemisorbed and physisorbed hydrogen. The term ‘physical adsorption’ implies that there is no energy 
barrier to ‘lock’ gas molecules out from such a surface, as depicted below in Fig. 6. As such, there is no activation step, 
and physical adsorption is fast kinetically except for diffusional limitation. Heterogeneous physisorption of molecular 
hydrogen is estimated to vary in a range from 1 to 10 kJ mol–1, which is ten times smaller than the values characteristic 
of chemisorption processes [33].

Due to the weak interaction of carbonaceous materials with hydrogen, substantial physisorption is only observed at 

low temperatures (< 273 K) and is unsuitable for application in ambient conditions.

The two mechanisms by which hydrogen is adsorbed on carbon nanomaterials are (i) the Kubas interaction and (ii) 
the spillover mechanism, both of which are well discussed by Nagar et al. [34]. The Kubas interaction mechanism involves 
the transfer of a charge from the highest occupied orbital of the  H2 ligand to the vacant metal d-orbitals, followed by 
a transfer back to the lowest unoccupied orbital of the ligand. Another mechanism known as spillover is described as

Different factors, namely surface area and pore structure, may also affect the hydrogen sorption mechanism in carbon-

surface and (2) hydrogen molecules permeating between the layers of carbon atoms [35]. Moreover, it has been reported

2.1.1   Physical activation of carbon materials for hydrogen storage

Commercial physical activation is a two-stage operation consisting of pyrolysis in a neutral atmosphere followed by 
activation in oxidizing atmospheric gases such as steam, carbon dioxide, carbon dioxide, and nitrogen or air mixtures at 
elevated temperatures in the interval of 800–1100 °C [37]. With this technique, it is possible to acquire activated carbon 
with a porous structure and excellent physical performance, which is considered a clean solution due to the absence of 
chemical agents [38]. In the process of physical activation of activated carbon, the prolonged activation time, the poor 
low adsorption capacity of the treated activated carbon, as well as excessive energy consumption are the major draw-
backs [39].

While physical activation has the advantage of not requiring corrosive and costly chemical as activators, resulting in 
lower production costs and a more environmentally friendly and simple operation, it presents challenges in accurately 
tuning the activation process and results in a relatively disordered porous structure [40].

The authors investigated the surface and pore structure properties and the hydrogen storage performance at ambient 
temperature of the super-activated carbon (SAC) materials fabricated by  CO2 activation of template porous carbons [41]. 
Activation is performed by placing the prepared carbon materials in the center of the quartz tube in the tube furnace, 
heating it to the activation temperature (1223 K) under nitrogen (5 K/min), followed by switching the gas flow to  CO2 
(30  cm3/min). After cooling to room temperature under nitrogen, the SAC sample was obtained after activation with 
 CO2. SAC materials were found to possess high specific surface areas of up to 2829  m2/g and large pore volumes of up 
to 2.34  cm3/g, much higher than unactivated materials.

In this [42], ACS samples were prepared from amorphous cellulose and characterized in texture and hydrogen adsorp-
tion. Samples were obtained by applying a physical activation pyrolysis method with two different pre-treatment steps, 
namely “cutting” (APAC) and “reducing in flakes” (AFPAC) methods, respectively. The activation reached 900 °C under con-
stant  CO2 flow. Most activated pores are smaller than 1 nm in diameter, with the mean value ranging from 0.5 to 0.6 nm,

2.1.2   Chemical activation of carbon materials

Chemical activation is a highly effective strategy for enhancing the hydrogen sorption properties of carbon materials 
derived from coal or biomass. This approach employs a single-step pyrolysis process conducted in the presence of a 
chemical activating agent. A range of chemical agents has been utilized for this purpose, including phosphoric acid, zinc 
chloride, and alkaline hydroxides such as KOH. It has been noted that alkaline hydroxides, particularly KOH, can yield 
materials with improved surface areas and pore volumes. High surface areas (> 2000  m2/g), large pore volume (about 
1  cm3/g), and uniform distribution of micropore sizes in the range of 1–2 nm and small mesopores are particularly char-
acteristic of activated carbons produced with KOH as the activating agent. The carbon structure is oxidized to generate 
carbonate ions and pores. Chemical activation offers multiple benefits, containing a reduced processing temperature, 
shorter reaction duration, and enhanced prevalence of micropores. However, it is hampered by the need to eliminate 
impurities produced during the activation procedure effectively. In the study conducted by [43] the wood samples 
were activated with KOH and phosphoric acid. They revealed that activated carbon has remarkably elevated levels of 
hydrogen absorption under nearly room temperature conditions and moderate pressures (up to 0.8 wt% at 25 °C and 
20 bar). It is also noted that the adsorption’s heat at zero coverage and the change in enthalpy throughout the gradual 
process showed substantial uptake levels, 10.9 kJ/mol and 17–20 kJ/mol, respectively. These results were unusual and 
exceeded the typical values reported for carbon-based materials previously [43]. The hydrothermal carbonization fol-
lowed by alkaline activation methods was used by Sangchoom et al. [44] and activated carbons (ACs) showed notable 
hydrogen absorption capacity, ranging from 3.6 to 6.2% at a pressure of 20 bar with a surface area of 3235  m2/g. In a 
recent study, activated carbon derived from biomass (Palimera sprout) with KOH activation accomplished a hydrogen 
uptake of approximately 1.06 wt% under conditions of room temperature and 15 bar [45]. Chemical activation is also 
applied to develop porosity in carbon nanofibers. Authors found that with only a specific surface area ranging from 
1500 to 1700  m2/g, it was possible to achieve a total hydrogen storage capacity of approximately 34 g  H2 per liter at a 
temperature of 77 K and pressure of 40 bar [46].

Most of the studies showed a positive effect of chemical activation on hydrogen storage capacity [47–49]. Application 
of the method allows biomass waste, food waste, and other carbon precursors to be utilized as hydrogen storage material.

2.1.3   Incorporation of elements or dopants/defects

Previous research showed that elements or dopants could be implemented to enrich reaction speed at mild conditions 
and achieve appropriate hydrogen sorption characteristics. Catalysts with high surface area contribute to altered surface 
interactions, dissociation of hydrogen molecules, and advanced sorption/desorption parameters.

The doping of catalysts is one of the most essential routes in enhancing the hydrogen adsorption/desorption 
kinetics of hydrogen storage devices. By inducing the rapid separation/bonding of hydrogen molecules/atoms, the 
critical role is to lift the hydrogen storage performance of the material. Catalyst doping of the carbon host can be 
seen in Fig. 7, which enhances hydrogen-carbon bond energy. Carbon nanomaterials can be altered by incorporating

One of the common strategies for modifying the physicochemical properties of carbon frameworks is heteroatom 
doping or substitution in the carbon matrix. The carbon atoms in the carbon structure are exchanged for heteroatoms, 
including boron/nitrogen/phosphorus/sulfur. Replacing the carbon in the carbon structure by heteroatoms may change 
the charge distribution and electronic properties of the carbon backbone because of their different size and electronega-
tivity relative to carbon, which can change how they interact with the reactants in electrocatalysis [58, 59]. The choice of 
synthesis strategies and parameters, such as temperature and pressure, is critical to achieving the desired physicochemi-
cal properties of the resulting heteroatom-doped carbon framework.

Nitrogen is the most widely used dopant among the various heteroatoms due to its five valence electrons and an 
atomic size comparable to carbon [60]. The higher electronegativity of nitrogen compared to that of carbon (3.04 > 2.55) 
activates polarization in the  sp2 hybridized carbon network, altering the physicochemical properties of carbon. Nitrogen-
doped graphene’s lattice structure has three configurations: pyridinic, pyrrolic, and graphitic-like nitrogen bonding. 
Primarily, pyridinic and graphitic-like nitrogen bonding is responsible for advancing the conductivity of graphene mate-
rials. There are various ways of N-doped graphene synthesis along with chemical vapor deposition (CVD) and solution 
plasma [61, 62].

Boron doping is another route to alter carbon materials’ physical features and chemical reactivity. Boron and nitrogen 
can straightly replace carbon atoms in the graphene lattice, leaving the original  sp2 hybridization and conjugated planar 
structure the same. The ability of boron to attract electrons leads to a p-doping effect that influences electrocatalytic 
activity. Studies show that B-doping enhances the uniform distribution of metal particles like Pd and Cu on the graphene 
framework, affecting the skeletal and electronic features of the compound [63, 64].

Due to its larger size and additional electron orbitals, Phosphorus has a fundamentally different doping effect than 
nitrogen. Its larger diameter compared to carbon can distort its structure and create defect sites in the graphene’s basal 
plane [65]. The result is a reduction in the electrical conductivity of the phosphorus-doped graphene material, which 
limits its use in specific applications.

Sulfur is considered another attractive doping heteroatom owing to its similar electronegativity (2.58) to carbon’s 
(2.55). S-doped graphene is shown to be negligibly polarized, which affects the change in the electronic arrangement of 
the graphene lattice. Another fact is that the dissimilarity between the sulfur and carbon orbitals because of non-uniform 
spin density distribution on sulfur-doped graphene materials results in some different catalytic characteristics valuable 
for specific applications [66]. Other promising features provided by C–S (-C = S/-C–S) bonds at the edge or near defects 
are advanced surface wettability, enhanced conductivity, and induced pseudo-capacitance due to created active sites 
[67, 68].

In the work of Subramaniam et al. [69] graphene oxide nanohybrids decorated with catalyst nanoparticles and the 
substrate (GO) doped with boron (B) demonstrated improved enthalpy of adsorption of molecular hydrogen on the 
substrate. The storage capacity of the Ni–B–rGO hybrid at the three temperatures (77 K, 273 K, and 298 K at 20 bar) is ~ 6.9 
wt%, ~ 0.41 wt%, and 0.16 wt%, respectively.

Together, their findings confirm that incorporating elements or dopants enhances the sorption features of storage 
materials, including kinetics and thermodynamic properties, owing to advanced electron transfer and surface-boundary 
reactions.

2.2   Nanostructuring and nanoconfinement of metal hydrides with carbon materials

Another way to overcome the kinetic barriers associated with diffusion is to move to nanostructured/nanoscale mate-
rials. The surface atoms in nanosized materials have high surface energy and can easily combine with other atoms to 
transform into stable states.

However, nanoscale materials are susceptible to accumulation and even sintering at elevated temperatures. For some 
hydrides, the synthesis of nanoparticles is very complicated in principle. By classifying the nanoparticles within the sup-
port material or so-called nanoconfinement, as shown in Fig. 8, the utilization of nanostructured supports is a viable 
way to impede particle growth and accumulation of the hydride, which also maintains the dehydrated products in close 
contact by restricting their mobility. In addition, the supporting material should be chemically inert, stable under the 
conditions necessary for hydrogen release and uptake, and sufficiently light to retain a high gravimetric hydrogen storage 
capacity for the nanocomposite. Furthermore, a support material with catalytic activity can facilitate hydrogen’s chemical 
desorption and absorption. Significant growth has been made in using nanomaterials as structural and catalytic supports 
to advance the hydrogen storage performance of various hydrides.

Multiple techniques for fabricating materials under nanoconfinement conditions, i.e., with size restrictions owing to the 
confined nanoscale volume, have been evolved to resolve these issues. Nanoconfinement was first used to enhance the 
kinetics of  NaAlH4 by placing the hydride in carbon aerogels [72]. Microporous activated carbon, graphene, polymeric and 
carbon nanotubes, hollow carbon nanospheres, metal–organic framework materials, etc., have also been used as limit-
ing frameworks [73]. Using theoretical and experimental methods, the authors reported  Li3N[LiNH2 + 2LiH] under nano-
confinement conditions in nanoporous carbon with pore size ~ 3 nm. They showed that the presence of nanosurfaces

3   Carbon materials for hydrogen storage

3.1   Zero‑dimensional nanostructured carbon materials

Zero-dimensional (0D) nanomaterials in the range of 0–100 nm, comprising graphene quantum dots (GQDs), carbon 
quantum dots (CQDs), fullerenes, inorganic quantum dots (QDs), have aroused significant attention due to their ultra-
small size, high specific surface area, quantum confinement effect, excellent physical and chemical properties. In contrast 
to bulk high dimensional nanomaterials, 0D nanomaterials are composed of spherical or quasi-spherical nanoparticles

handling dispersion interactions, finite temperature effects, large system sizes, and realistic environmental conditions 
might make it less suitable for providing precise predictions for practical applications.

[98]. According to XRD data, all samples show diffraction peaks at 43.9°, 51.2° and 75.4° assigned to NiFe alloy, while

these findings, CNTs with a special structure supported by transition metal catalysts are essential in heterogeneous 
catalysis in Mg-based hydrogen storage. NiFe particles are warped by the carbon at the top, and the wall thickness 
of synthesized CNT is much lower.

isorptive hydrogen storage mechanism at room temperature. In this respect, an array of functionalized CNTs is fabricated 
and exposed to extensive material characterization techniques and hydrogen storage measurements. Increased rough-
ness and apparent defects at the side walls increased after treating MWCNTs in the mixture of  H2SO4:HNO3. The highest 
interlayer spacing, oxygen/carbon ratio (26.09 at%), defect content, and specific surface area (215.3  m2/g) were found 
for the  H2SO4:HNO3 functionalized sample at 100 °C. The modifications mentioned above were crucial in increasing the 
hydrogen storage capacity of CNTs by ~ 150% at 298 K and 50 bar, with 51% hydrogen reversibility. The study showed that 
hydrogen molecules with a kinetic diameter of 2.89 Å could enter the increased interlayer spacing and move or diffuse 
between the layers. In summary, the presence of oxygen functional groups and defects is responsible for the additional 
hydrogen storage density since the enhancement in hydrogen absorption was more significant than the expansion in 
the surface area of the specimen.

provide a better structural condition for producing activated carbon hollow fibers. The resulting specimen has a relatively 
smooth outer-walled structure. The inner walled structure is dispersed with micron-sized macropores (0.31–2.18 μm). 
The benefits of the obtained compound rely on abundant micro-/mesoporous structure (0–6 nm) and oxygen-/nitrogen- 
functional groups. The surface oxygen functionalities are predominantly C–O, C = O, O = C–O, and P = O, and the surface 
nitrogen functionalities are predominantly pyridine, N–H,  NH4+, and  NO2. Its multi-stage pore structure and abundant 
surface functional groups provide excellent physical and structural conditions for hydrogen storage. At atmospheric pres-
sure, the hydrogen uptake of N/O-ACHF is equal to 1.35 wt%. Various transition metal-based nanocatalysts adsorbed on 
the CNT surface are considered to improve the properties of CNTs [18, 99–101]. The chemical dissociation of hydrogen 
molecules by adsorbed nanocatalysts enhances the storage of hydrogen atoms on the CNT surface [18, 99]. CNTs doped

All in all, 1D nanostructures maintain great solid-state storage of hydrogen and alter hydrogen adsorption capacity by 
enhancing adsorption/desorption cycles. Hydrogen storage mechanisms of these materials is based on physisorption 
and spillover effect, where high surface area and curvature enable moderate hydrogen adsorption and they can act as 
a bridge for hydrogen spillover from a catalyst. The drawbacks of 1D nanomaterials hinder their practical application, 
notably inadequate sorption and desorption at high temperatures and the expense of their manufacture. Decorating 
CNTs with metals or metal oxides creates additional active sites and enhances hydrogen binding energy through chem-
isorption or physisorption. In the Table 3, hydrogenation properties of 1D materials with storage capacities reaching 
1.35–5.14 wt% at 77 K in the ambient-higher pressure, respectively are shown. Introducing elements such as nickel, 
nitrogen and  La2O3 into 1D carbon materials has been shown to significantly enhance their hydrogen storage capacity. 
Yet, high-pressure and low-temperature conditions are required to achieve appreciable hydrogen storage capacities for 
most of the works in Table 3. Pristine CNTs have a tendency to aggregate due to van der Waals forces. Decorating CNTs 
with nanoparticles or functional groups introduces steric hindrance, preventing aggregation and ensuring uniform dis-
persion, which improves overall stability. Recent advances in using different one-dimensional nanomaterials and their 
compounds in hydrogen storage, which were discussed in detail in this review, illustrate the progress made over the 
recent years in fabrication methods.

According to a study by Patchkovskii et al. [110], by increasing the interlayer spacing of graphene from 6 to 8 Å, it 
is possible to enhance the storage capacity from 2–3%, achieving a range of 5.0–6.5 wt% of hydrogen at an operating 
pressure of 5 MPa. An early study by Carrete et al. [111] was reported that replacing graphene nanosheets with Al atoms 
could enhance hydrogen storage capacity. Graphene nanoribbons (GNRs) can be defined as strips of graphene. In GNRs 
featuring hydrogen-passivated edges, the spins are aligned in a zigzag pattern along each edge, exhibiting metallic or 
semiconducting behavior contingent on the alignment of spins at the edge pairs. However, their results did not satisfy 
DOE targets.

The present work [19] studies the effect of Al doping on the electronic states of graphene using DFT calculations. 
A chemical bond is formed between the  Al3+ ion and the hexagonal site of the benzene ring of graphene nanoflakes 
(GR). Diffusion of the Al species from one hexagonal site to the next occurs via the C–C bond center of benzene rings. 
The  Al3+ ion height was found to be 2.406 Å from the GR surface, with an observed increase in height corresponding to 
an incremental rise in Al charge (from + 1 to + 3). This phenomenon can be attributed to the observation that the posi-
tive charge of GR increases in tandem with the charge of Al. Consequently, the repulsive interaction between Al + and 
GR + intensifies with the growth of the valence charge. Figure 14 illustrates the structures of  H2 adsorbed on GR-Al 
(GR19-Al3 + -(H2)n, n = 1–4). When n = 1,  H2 is bonded to Al with a side-by-side arrangement, where the two hydrogen 
atoms of  H2 are bonded to Al with near-equal distances (R1 = 2.445 Å, R10 = 2.415 Å). The second  H2 molecule,  (H2)2, is 
bonded to Al with a similar side-by-side configuration with n = 2. The hydrogen binding energy to GR-Al3 + was equal to 
0.7 kcal/mol, which is considered low. The doping of GR with Al ions results in the formation of new electronic bands in 
the low-energy regions, suggesting the possibility of electronic applications.

In the work of Luhadiya et al. [56], the authors investigated the hydrogen adsorption behavior of functionalized Ti 
and N-doped graphene sheets containing a variety of defects (D–G) using molecular dynamics (MD) simulations. In 
particular, graphene sheets with monovacancy, Stone–Wales, and multiple double vacancies. The research showed that 
the hydrogen adsorption capacity of the graphene sheets improved significantly as the concentration of Ti atoms on 
the D-G sheets increased. Due to DV(III)-G sheets having a small number of large pores that bind hydrogen with high 
binding energy, the adsorption capacity of DV(III)-G sheets is maximal at 300 K. The N doping on the D–G sheets initially 
reduced their hydrogen adsorptive capacity, but the N–D–G sheets increased their hydrogen adsorptive capacity with 
increasing Ti atom concentrations. The Ti-N-DV(III)-G sheet with a Ti concentration of 10.5% showed a hydrogen uptake 
of 5.5 wt% compared to all other defect types at 300 K and 100 bar pressure.

Currently, the properties of cobalt alloys are not suitable for use in this area, and their ability to preserve hydrogen 
will need to be subsequently strengthened. As a substitute for noble metal doping, graphene was doped with two 
non-metallic elements (nitrogen and sulfur) by hydrothermal technique [113]. The experimental findings reveal that, in 
contrast with the single-element doping, the electrode co-doped with sulfur and nitrogen acquires greater values in the 
electrochemical storage of hydrogen. Since nitrogen atoms can provide more active centers in graphene, the discharge 
capacity cycle stability of NSG-doped alloys is better than that of GO-doped and NG-doped alloys that are appropriate 
for hydrogen storage. Its large specific surface area provides more reaction sites for hydrogen to diffuse, and its excellent 
conductivity enhances interfacial charge transfer. The sulfur in graphene contains a larger atomic size than the nitrogen, 
raises the polarization, and prompts an increased density of electrons in the graphene network.

The one-step hydrothermal synthesis of  CeVO4/rGO nanocomposites is expected to enhance hydrogen storage effi-
ciency owing to their unique features, such as appropriate electrochemical behavior, high specific surface area, and 
good porosity [22]. As well as controlling  CeVO4 nanoparticle growth, hydrazine is responsible for reducing graphitic 
oxides (GO) to reduced graphite oxides (rGO), allowing a single-step synthesis. Storage results indicated that adding 
graphene enhanced interlayer synergy, increasing hydrogen storage capacity. Compared to other nanostructures, the 
highest electrochemical hydrogen storage was achieved in the fabricated nanocomposite with the largest surface area 
and volume of pores. Research has shown that pore size is a very effective determinant of hydrogen storage capacity. 
The amount of hydrogen uptake is substantially raised due to the stronger hydrogen bonds formed in the smaller pores. 
Fine-grained and mesoporous materials have been reported to be promising for hydrogen storage. The application of 
porous fine-grained materials is limited due to the slow mass transfer rate, whereas mesoporous materials overcome 
this limitation. The smaller the pore diameter, the larger the surface area needed to absorb hydrogen, which is evident.
Using a straightforward and innovative hydrothermal route, the ternary solid phase of  UO3⋅NH3H2O has been efficiently 
manufactured in an ammoniated environment [114]. Uranium may serve as a powerful chemical store for hydrogen, 
which contains nearly twice the weight of gas by volume of liquefied hydrogen. In addition, the strong interactions 
between the graphene matrix and the metal oxide nanoparticles are exciting. Hydrogen adsorption on uranium-doped 
graphene nanosheets was the area of interest of Vanik Ghoulipoura et al. [115] and he found that, in addition to ura-
nium’s significant propensity for interaction with graphene, the obtained U-decorated graphene nanoparticles perform 
hydrogen adsorption storage surfaces. The hydrogen storage capacity for graphene oxide was only 2.30 wt%, whereas 
by adding  UO3⋅NH3H2O nanoparticles in GO, it was 61.46% by weight. As the number of cycles and repetitions rise, the 
amount and power of hydrogen storage escalates in all samples, likely due to the formation of new empty sites that 
foster hydrogen adsorption.

For developing novel energy materials, efficient engineering strategies to synthesize hydrides with high capacity 
and favorable reversibility are essential. In this work [119], by confinement on graphene via a solution self-confinement 
method, a nano-sized Mg-based borohydride, Mg(BH4)2, having a stable structure, has been fabricated. With a layer of 
8.8 nm (Fig. 14c), graphene-bonded Mg(BH4)2 displays a crumpled 2D nanosheet pattern according to Fig. 15a, b. The 
wrinkly morphology of 2D Mg(BH4)2@GR is less clear than that of GR. This observation suggests that the successful 
confinement of Mg(BH4)2 is the reason for this phenomenon, which was previously studied by Han et al. [120]. With a 
superior capacity of 12.0 wt.%, such 2D nano-Mg(BH4)2 can start dehydrogenation at 67.9 °C and 100 bars of hydrogen 
pressure, which is 190.5 °C lower than pure Mg(BH4)2. According to isothermal dehydrogenation tests and kinetic fitting 
results, the 2D composite has significantly upgraded dehydrogenation kinetics, with an activation energy of 31.3 kJ/
mol. Theoretical calculations of Mg(BH4)2 and the graphene-bound intermediate  MgB12H12, the charge transfer state 
of both samples is modified to facilitate de/rehydrogenation, resulting in substantial thermodynamic improvements in 
reversible hydrogen storage performance for graphene composite.

Graphene-supported nickel catalysts were discovered to ameliorate alloy particle size and grain size uniformity, declin-
ing the hydrogen-releasing temperature of the composite by approximately 90 °C. For the synthesis of the  CeMg12/Ni 
alloy, the mechanical ball milling method was employed [121]. The broadening of the diffraction peaks of the alloy with 
increasing graphene content can be seen from the diffraction peak analysis. The gradual widening of the diffractometric 
peak suggests that the addition of graphene in the process of ball milling of the alloy helps to refine the alloy particles, 
thus increasing the alloys’ internal specific surface area and hydrogen diffusion channel and strengthen the dissolution 
of Ni in the primary state of the alloy. By lowering the thermal stability of the alloy hydride, the addition of graphene 
reinforces its dehydrogenation performance. Adding graphene is advantageous in building folded or granular features 
on the surface of the particles and enhancing surface activity. It has been shown that the ratio of ID to IG directly reflects 
the change in the surface defects of the treated specimen, increasing the pore density and the surface activity of the alloy 
by bonding to the surface of the alloy grains. Based on the lowest activation energy for dehydrogenation of 85.23 kJ/
mol and a special dehydrogenation time of 1090 s, superior dehydrogenation kinetic performances were obtained for 
the alloy with 6 wt% graphene.

In summary, various modified graphene structures, such as decorated graphene, doped graphene, vacancy-doped 
graphene, vacancy-doped, and decorated-doped graphene, have been investigated to modify the reactivity of pristine 
graphene. Hydrogen storage of these mechanisms based on physisorption and chemisorption, where large specific area 
follows for efficient hydrogen adsorption and hydrogen atoms can chemisorb to the graphene surface or edges. Advan-

as well as easy chemical modifies (e.g. doping with metals or heteroatoms). Table 4 reviews the hydrogenation properties 
of 2D materials reaching about 5.16–14.13 wt% from ambient temperature to 300 °C, respectively. When combined with 
other storage materials (e.g., metal hydrides), decorated graphene enhances overall hydrogen storage performance.

3.4   Three‑dimensional nanostructured carbon materials

Alternatively to CNT and graphene, 3D-based carbon composites can extend the dimensions along all three directions. 
In addition to well-studied 3D nanomaterials, containing mesoporous carbon and activated carbon (AC) [126], there are 
novel types of carbonaceous materials which can assemble CNTs and graphene. Plenty of 3D nanocarbon structures, 
such as vertically aligned CNTs [127], sponges [128], foams [129], graphene arrays [130], graphene foams [131], etc., can 
be synthesized in an attempt to create novel materials for hydrogen storage. The merits of 3D carbon nanostructured 
materials for hydrogen storage comprise characteristics of 1D and 2D nanomaterials, such as outstanding conductivity, 
high charge transport, excellent surface area, and durability. Besides, these materials offer new hierarchical structures 
and minimize transition resistance.

Ongoing research is being undertaken to develop and characterize multifunctional materials for energy and environ-
mental applications. A recent study by N. Kostoglou et al. [23] is concluded that a nanoporous polymeric/polyaniline-
derived activated carbon (PDAC) with a large surface area (~ 2200  m2/g) and pore volume (~ 1  m3/g) has been exten-
sively investigated for its potential use in  H2 storage and supercapacitor energy storage. Coral-like fibers with diameters 
between 100 and 200 nm and a foam-like porous structure for the former were observed for the freeze-dried polymer 
and commercial activated carbon (YP80F). According to the signal-to-noise ratio, the high-frequency region showed a 
comprehensive feature consisting of two components—the 2D band at ~ 2700 cm-1, due to second-order scattering 
processes, and the combination D + D’ defect-activated mode at ~ 2900  cm-1. A turbostratic structure with significant 
distortions in the stacking of the graphene sheets is suggested by the absence of a pronounced 2D band. The average 
porosity is significantly smaller in PDAC than in the YP80F reference, indicating significantly smaller pores in PDAC [132]. 
PDAC exhibited a completely reversible type I(a) isotherm, as classified by IUPAC [133], with a distinct saturation plateau, 
indicating a purely microporous material (< 2 nm pore size). The shape of the YP80F isotherm is more characteristic of 
the I(b) type, which is the IUPAC classification for microporous materials with a broader distribution. The PDAC achieved 
a high and completely reversible gravimetric excess  H2 uptake of ~ 5.5 wt.% at 77 K and ~ 60 bar, together with the heat 
of adsorption of ~ 8.3 kJ/mol at zero coverage, indicating excellent  H2 adsorption efficiency at low temperatures.

A novel process for the preparation of porous carbon materials from the vapors of biomass pyrolysis using a calcium 
citrate template has been proposed [134]. The effects of pyrolytic temperature, pyrolytic heating rate, and carbonaceous 
precursor preparation temperature on biomass pyrolytic product yield, composition of light biofuel, and porous carbon 
structure have been studied. As the heating rate increases, the specific surface area and volume of the porosity of the 
carbon increases and decreases, peaking around 10 K/min. Simultaneously, the microporosity exhibits a rising trend 
and remains almost unchanged after 10 K/min. Porosity in carbon materials prepared by CaO template process can be 
attributed to removing nano-CaO and internal activation by  CO2 and  H2O. Slow heating rates, e.g., 2 K/min, produce low 
pyrolysis steam and excess calcium citrate in the carbonaceous feedstock. This leads to overdevelopment of the pore 
structure of BG-2, with macro- and mesopores dominating. This allows the complete mixing of pyrolysis fumes and cal-
cium citrate, promoting the formation of a mesoporous and microporous pore structure in the subsequent carbonation. 
If the heating speed is too fast, too much steam is produced, and the quality of the pores is reduced. Optimal pyrolytic 
temperature (823 K), heating rate (10 K/min), and carbonaceous precursor preparation temperature (473 K), the manu-
factured porous carbon material has the largest specific surface area of 1703  m2/g, a relatively high microvoid volume 
of 0.51  cm3/g and a microporosity of 24.17%. At 77 K at atmospheric pressure, the  H2 adsorptive capacity of the carbon 
material can be as high as 170.12  cm3/g (1.53 wt%).

This study [24] conveys the use of a novel three-dimensional graphene structure that can overcome the limitations of 
the two-dimensional nature of graphene and its application in hydrogen absorption. These findings evidence hydrogen 
bonding on single-layer graphene conformally grown by the epitaxial growth method on the (0001) face of a porous 
4H-SiC wafer. Due to its two-dimensional nature, hydrogen storage devices based on pristine flat graphene would require 
prohibitively large surfaces. Graphene can be folded into 3D compact structures that retain its outstanding properties. 
These atoms rearrange themselves into graphene’s characteristic hexagonal geometry. The first layer formed is the so-
called buffer layer, where 30% of the C atoms are covalently bonded to Si atoms. Subsequent sublimation of Si results 
in the growth of the second buffer layer, separating the first layer and transforming the latter into a single layer of free-
standing graphene. Van der Waals interactions are the only way the resulting layer is bonded to the substrate. The mor-
phology of the 3D substrate is closely followed by the graphene layers grown by this method. They form a meandering

Of all the transition metal catalysts, Fe effectually modulates the de/rehydrogenation features of  MgH2 [25]. The usage 
of an appropriate support for the scaffolding/nanoconfinement of nanoparticles can assist to alleviate the agglomeration 
of Fe particles [135]. A proper support for metallic catalysts has been discovered to be hollow carbon spheres (HCS) due 
to their mesoporous nature. One-pot methods can manufacture a highly porous carbon network [136, 137]. Depending 
on their shape and size, HCS structure significantly affects hydrogen sorption properties (a high BET value, voids, hol-
low spaces, doping). To enhance these features, the defects and thin walls can be created to increase the amount of  H2 
in HCS. This work found HCS in sizes between 200 and 500 nm with an interconnecting tubular network with pore size 
between 10 and 25 nm. The high-pressure hysteresis loop shows that HCS contains large pores ranging from mesopores 
to macropores. The TEM image shows that the  MgH2 particles are trapped inside the HCS together with the tiny Fe parti-
cles. A clear indication of the interaction between the Fe nanoparticles and the carbon atoms of the HCS is the formation 
of the Fe3C phase. This interaction is expected to prevent the accumulation of Fe particles during de/rehydrogenation 
by keeping the Fe particles intact with the HCS. This is a favorable environment for the synergistic enhancement of the 
sorption properties of  MgH2. The initial desorption temperature for  MgH2 catalyzed by hollow carbon spheres and Fe 
nanoparticles  (MgH2-Fe-HCS) was observed to be 225.9 °C with a hydrogen storage capacity of 5.60 wt%.

Enriching hydrogen storage in 3D graphene remains to be explored, with metal atoms being added to functionalize the 
material, such as Pd, Pt, or Ti, which have already been proven to improve hydrogen storage in flat graphene [138–140]. 
Decorated Pt–Co bimetallic nanoparticles on N-doped mesoporous carbon (Pt–Co@NMC) were developed to improve 
performance [141], whereas Co was added to increase capacity and Pt to enhance kinetic performance. The specimens 
showed a standard IV isotherm and a type  H2 hysteresis loop, reflecting a mesoporous nature and cage-like pores (3 mm) 
with small entries. 2% Pt–Co@NMC composite contains many defect sites, which may positively affect hydrogen storage. 
This was reported according to the integrated intensity ratio of D and G bands of 1.27, which value was high enough. The 
neighboring N doping, which can introduce more defects, provide more active sites, and increase the insertion of H atoms 
into the carbon composites, will also affect the carbon atoms’ spin density and charge distribution. All the samples were 
similarly spherical, and those with platinum inlays were rough, and the particles were agglomerated. The carbon matrix 
encapsulates the metal particles, as the high-magnification SEM images show. This carbon-covered metal structure offers 
excellent advantages regarding hydrogen storage capacity and may delay or even prevent metal particle aggregation 
during charging and discharging to some degree. Significant elements in enhancing the electrochemical performance 
of hydrogen storage are the synergistic effect of metallic cobalt and platinum and the highly dispersed metallic Co and 
Pt nanoparticles in the carbon composite material.

Hydride-graphite composites have obtained considerable focus due to their elevated thermal conductivities [142]. 
Milling the alloy with nano graphite (NG) powder, nanocomposite materials with unique microstructures of nano-sized 
graphite flakes and graphene-embedded and supported nanocrystalline-amorphous alloys can be fabricated [143, 144]. 
 Sm5Mg41 + x wt% nano-graphite (NG) (x = 0, 2, 4, 8, 12) components are synthesized via ball-milling [145]. As a result of 
grinding and NG doping, the intensity of the hydrogen absorber/desorber peak decreases, and the peak width increases, 
resulting in a significantly smaller powder size and storage of strain energy, contributing to hydrogen desorption. Mg 
produced by ball milling is easily precipitated on the surface of nano graphite due to its good thermal conductivity 
and large specific surface area. Furthermore, many microstructural defects, such as nanocrystalline grain boundaries, 
dislocations, sub-grain boundaries, and micro-twins, are seen, resulting from crushing and cold welding during milling. 
As the nano graphite content rises, an increasing number of nanocrystalline Mg phases appear on the surface of the NG 
sheets as shown in Fig. 16a–c. NG has been found on the surface of hydrogen storage alloys, forming an extremely stable 
composite. Many NG nanosheets are embedded in the alloy, introducing more nanosurfaces into the composites. It is 
found that nano-interfaces of NG exert a structural constraint on  MgH2 nanocrystal growth during hydrogen absorption 
and that nanocrystals dominate composite microstructure after hydrogen absorption. This helps attain a substantial 
outcome on the Mg-based alloy’s hydrogen hydriding and dehydriding reaction.

Carbon aerogels are highly encouraging for hydrogen storage due to their lightweight, porous structure and tunable 
properties. Pure carbon aerogels rely on physisorption, which is less efficient at room temperature Enhancements via 
doping or functionalization are requmeired to enhance surface properties and resolve temperature-dependent limita-
tions. In the work of Cheng et al. [148], incorporating nitrogen and nickel nanoparticles enhances binding energy and 
storage performance, exhibiting hydrogen storage capacity of 7.4 wt% at 77 K. The morphological study showed that the 
material is primarily composed of micro- and mesopores. Due to weak hydrogen-surface interactions at 298 K, storage 
experiments are conducted at 77 K to meet the DOE’s 5.5 wt% target. However, at this low temperature, hydrogen dis-
sociation from metal ions becomes challenging, leading to reduced storage capacity with increased Ni particle loading. 
The CAs quantity was kept constant while varying the Ni dopant mass percentages, producing samples labeled NixN2-
CAs (x = 1, 2, 5, 10). The Ni1N2 sample achieved a hydrogen storage capacity of 7.4 wt%, 25% higher than the original 5.9 
wt%. This improvement is attributed to nitrogen doping, which altered the charge distribution around nitrogen atoms, 
enhancing hydrogen interactions.

Table 5 outlines the hydrogen absorption properties of carbon nanomaterials within the 3D morphologies for vari-
ous hydrogen storage systems. The collected data analysis demonstrates that carbon nanomaterials can be applied as 
catalysts, coating layers, substrates, etc. The different dimensionality of carbon materials, their synthesis routes, hydrogen 
uptake, wt.% (in some cases electrochemical performance based on discharge capacity), conditions of absorption/des-
orption cycles, and required time are illustrated. According to Table 5, maximum hydrogen storage capacity of 10.2 wt%. 
is reached at 77 K and 55 bars, while at 25–340 °C hydrogen sorption capacities vary from 3,15 to 3,75 wt% in the pres-
sure range of 0–75 bars. At room temperature, the weak hydrogen-carbon interaction is insufficient to retain hydrogen 
molecules effectively. However, at 77 K, the reduced kinetic energy of hydrogen molecules enables efficient physisorp-
tion, leveraging the large surface area and microporous structure of 3D materials [149]. At cryogenic temperatures, the 
high surface area of 2D materials may not fully compensate for their lack of a 3D interconnected structure, limiting gas 
diffusion and storage. However, at room temperature, their functionalized surfaces enable stronger hydrogen binding, 
making them more effective for ambient storage applications [150, 151].

In summary, 3D carbon-based materials for hydrogen storage maintain characteristics of 1D and 2D nanomateri-
als. The material offers significant advantages, including high volumetric and gravimetric hydrogen storage capacities, 
extensive tunability of pore size and distribution, and scalable, cost-efficient production techniques, such as those utiliz-
ing biomass. The drawbacks associated with 3D materials encompass lower electronic conductivity compared to their 
2D counterparts, and the critical need for pore size optimization to enrich adsorption performance. Carbon aerogels 
provide hierarchical porosity and outstanding cryogenic storage potential, whereas porous carbon materials are both 
cost-effective and easily scalable. Future research will likely focus on optimizing their properties through functionaliza-
tion and hybridization with other materials to achieve practical hydrogen storage systems.

4   Summary and outlook

This review summarizes the various routes for the design and synthesis of carbon nanomaterials that have been devel-
oped and studied extensively for their application in the field of hydrogen storage. Research on carbon nanomaterials 
has continually attracted significant attention and has resulted in pivotal advances. They are highly sought-after in a 
variety of fields, including lithium-ion battery materials, optoelectronic materials, catalyst carriers, chemical and biological 
sensors, hydrogen storage materials, supercapacitor materials, and other significant applications due to their distinctive 
structure and exceptional physical and chemical properties. Generally, carbon materials ranging from 0D to 3D are con-
sidered promising hydrogen storage materials owing to their chemical stability, low molar mass, high surface area, and 
variations of different forms and structures. The surface area of carbonaceous materials is regarded as one of the pivotal 
aspects of hydrogen sorption properties since hydrogen storage capacity is proportional to a given area. Taking this into 
consideration, efficient hydrogen storage via carbon-based materials is established on porous spatial structures along 
with high surface area. Thus, structural and spatial alterations or catalytic enhancements of carbon-based materials are 
necessary for building safe, reliable, and high-surface-area hydrogen storage systems working at moderate conditions.
The activity of carbon materials for hydrogen storage varies significantly depending on their dimensional structure. 
These discrepancies arise due to variations in surface area, pore structure, electronic properties, and interaction mecha-
nisms with hydrogen. For most practical hydrogen storage applications, 3D carbon materials are the best option due to 
their balance of high storage capacity, scalability, and cost-effectiveness. They are particularly effective for physisorption-

storage, 2D carbon materials offer a promising path forward, provided the challenges of aggregation and cost can be 
addressed. For room-temperature storage, 2D carbon materials are promising due to their functionalized surfaces, which 
enable stronger hydrogen binding, despite hindrances like aggregation and cost. However, at cryogenic temperatures, 
their lack of a 3D interconnected structure limits gas diffusion and storage efficiency.

Currently, the best hydrogen storage capacity range for carbon-based materials lies between 4.65 and 6.5 wt% 
obtained experimentally at ambient conditions. However, studies using DFT and Monte Carlo calculations show higher 
values up to 8 wt%.

Creating affordable materials and techniques that possess the necessary kinetics and thermodynamics is a primary 

obstacle in the field of hydrogen storage technologies. The review highlights some main points:

1.  The most prevalently used methods to improve hydrogen storage characteristics are incorporation of different ele-
ments/catalysts, nanostructuring and nanoconfinement, and chemical and physical activation of biomass and coal-
based carbons.

2.  Several studies based on carbon structures, entailing graphene, graphite, nanotube, and fullerene, have been inves-

tigated for hydrogen storage, involving DFT studies, and promising results have been acquired.

3.  As a result, various approaches, such as defect engineering and surface functionalization, have been applied to 
enforce the hydrogen storage properties of these structures. These strategies allow us to improve hydrogen storage 
in carbon structures such as graphene, carbon nanotubes, and fullerenes.

4.  Nanostructuring has improved the surface area of carbonaceous materials. It also affects better hydrogen storage 

capacities due to the formation of nanosized pores.

The ultimate objective is to craft carbon-based materials capable of achieving a hydrogen storage capacity of around 
6.5 wt% while maintaining the essential adsorption/desorption rate under standard room temperature and pressure con-
ditions. Although some materials have potential storage capacities, difficulties still exist in properly integrating carbon-
based materials with hydrogen storage technologies. Therefore, addressing upcoming issues should be a primary focus.
